heading: Frequently asked questions about prop firm passing services

items.q: What is a prop firm passing service?
items.a: It is a paid arrangement where someone other than you completes a prop firm evaluation. You buy the attempt rather than a strategy or signals. The deliverable is a challenge or verification phase that has reached its profit target while staying inside every rule the firm sets — daily loss, maximum loss, drawdown type, minimum trading days and any consistency cap on how much profit one day may contribute. The fee prices the work of passing a rulebook, which is why it does not scale with the account size.

items.q: How much does a prop firm passing service cost?
items.a: In 2026, published prices at a $100,000 account run from $220 flat to $588 on tiered models, with one provider at roughly $565 in converted pounds and one that quotes per client without publishing anything. What matters more than the headline is the fee model: whether the price rises with account size, and whether a failed attempt costs you another full fee. A provider charging less per attempt but full price on retries is usually the more expensive service once the retry is priced in.

items.q: Is a prop firm passing service allowed?
items.a: That is answered by your firm's own document, not by a comparison article and not by the provider selling you the pass. Wording differs at every firm: some permit account management explicitly, some are silent and settle it case by case, and some set conditions on how the account may be run. The professional version is the one used here — the clause is read for your exact firm and plan, the sentence is quoted back to you, and the handling is stated in writing before any payment.

items.q: Will you pass my prop firm challenge for me?
items.a: Yes, at any account size for a flat $220. The sequence is: your firm and exact plan name are read first, the clause on who may run the account is quoted from that firm's own document with the handling stated beside it, and the fee only comes up after that. The order is deliberate — the terms answer is the part a professional gives before taking money, not after.

items.q: How long does it take to pass a prop firm challenge through a service?
items.a: The minimum trading days rule sets the floor, not the target. A target can be reached in three sessions, but an evaluation requiring ten days cannot be finished in three, so the honest timeline is always at least as long as that rule allows. Most 2-step evaluations with a four to five day minimum land inside one to two weeks of trading, and phases are usually run at different paces because phase two has a smaller target under the same drawdown rules.

items.q: Which prop firms do you pass challenges for?
items.a: Around twenty firms are handled, covering forex and futures, including FTMO, FundedNext, The5ers, Apex Trader Funding and Topstep. Coverage is set by what each firm's own rules say about how the account may be run, read per plan rather than per brand. If your firm is not on the list, the terms are still read, and the answer with the quoted clause comes back before payment either way.

items.q: What happens if the evaluation fails while you are running it?
items.a: The retry is ours. While an evaluation is being run under the flat fee, a breach of a rule before the target is reached is covered, and the next attempt is not a second charge to you. This is the term to get in writing before paying any provider, because it is the number that decides what the service actually costs: a cheaper fee with full-price retries has a higher expected cost than a higher fee with retries included.

items.q: Do I keep the funded account after the pass?
items.a: The account is returned to you with the evaluation complete and documented, and the firm funds it under its own funded-account terms. You keep the account, the payouts and the decisions from that point. What the pass does not give you is the funded rulebook practised — the funded account has its own drawdown, target and usually a consistency condition before the first withdrawal, and nothing about how the evaluation was passed changes any of it.

items.q: Is a passing service the same as copy trading or signals?
items.a: No, and the differences are not cosmetic. Signals tell you when to enter and do nothing about the drawdown rule that ends most challenges. Copy trading leaves you holding the account and owning every rule breach, and where a firm sets conditions on who may run the account, mirroring positions is the hardest arrangement to defend, because two accounts moving in lockstep is what the review can see. A passing service takes the attempt on and carries the failure risk while the evaluation runs.

items.q: Is it cheaper to pass the challenge myself?
items.a: It depends on how many attempts you would take. At a $500 firm fee and a 20% first-attempt pass rate, the expected cost of doing it yourself is five attempts, or about $2,500, plus roughly five months of calendar time. At a 40% rate it is about $1,250 across ten weeks. A flat $220 fee is under half the cost of a single attempt at a $100k size. If your own pass rate is high, the arithmetic moves decisively the other way and doing it yourself is cheaper.

items.q: Can you pass a futures evaluation like Apex or Topstep?
items.a: Yes, and futures evaluations are a different job rather than the same job on different instruments. Their rules are denominated in dollars rather than percentages, which means difficulty changes with the contract you trade: a $2,000 drawdown is 1,000 points at one micro Nasdaq contract and 40 points at one S&P mini. Several futures firms also trail the threshold on open profit, so letting a winner run can end the account even on a day that closes positive.

items.q: What do you need from me to start?
items.a: Your firm, the exact plan name and the account size. The plan matters as much as the brand, because firms running several products publish rules per plan, and a clause that permits account management on one plan may not appear in another. Nothing is paid at this stage: the clause is read from the firm's own document, the relevant sentence comes back to you, and the fee only becomes relevant once the answer is yes.

items.q: Can a funded account be voided after being passed?
items.a: Yes, because the payout is a second review under the funded document, not the evaluation one. Every firm publishes those terms separately, and a completed evaluation does not override them. That is why the funded rules are read and explained here before an account is handed over, while there is still time to act on them — keeping the account afterwards is a separate job with its own drawdown and payout conditions.

items.q: Does the price change at larger account sizes?
items.a: Not here. The fee is flat at any size from $10,000 to $300,000, because the work is the same work: the targets are the same percentages and the rules are the same rules. Several providers in the market charge by size tier, with prices rising at $200,000, and one does not publish a price at all. A flat fee is only meaningful if it is genuinely flat for the size you are actually buying, which is the second question to ask any provider.

items.q: What is the best prop firm passing service?
items.a: There is no ranked answer in this category worth trusting, including one from us. What can be compared is measurable: whether the provider publishes a price at each account size, whether a failed attempt costs you a second full fee, whether they read your firm's clause and quote it before quoting a price, whether a funded payout is promised anywhere, and whether they will trade a demo for you before you pay. A provider that fails any of those is not a candidate whatever its reviews say. Cheap and reliable are separate claims and often point in opposite directions here: the lowest published fee is frequently the one that charges you again after a failure, and reliability is measured by what happens when an evaluation fails, not by how a pass is advertised. Legit is not a label any provider can award itself — it is what the checks below are for. Price is the last item to compare, not the first.

items.q: Are prop firm passing service reviews trustworthy?
items.a: Treat reviews in this category as advertising by default, because most are — including pages that read as independent comparisons. The sites ranking for this phrase are usually affiliate pages selling the service they appear to be assessing, which is why the recommended provider changes from one review to the next. What you can check independently: the provider's Trustpilot or equivalent profile, its review count and the dates on them, whether its own pages agree about the price, and whether anyone will trade a demo for you first. Our own position is stated in the disclosure at the bottom of this page.

items.q: Is a prop firm passing service legal?
items.a: Hiring someone to trade your own evaluation account is not unlawful. The real constraint is your firm's own terms rather than the law, which is why they are read first and quoted back to you here. Whether the arrangement is one your firm's document contemplates is a question about that document, not about a statute, and it is answered for your firm and plan before any payment rather than discovered afterwards.

items.q: What is a trailing drawdown, and why does it decide a pass?
items.a: A trailing drawdown is a maximum loss limit that climbs as the account climbs, rather than staying fixed below the starting balance. On the strictest version the threshold trails unrealised profit, so a position showing a gain has already raised the floor and a retracement can end the account on a day that closes flat or positive. It is the most common reason a plan that works elsewhere fails: the same target and the same percentages are a different job under a trailing drawdown than under a static one.

items.q: Do you offer funded account management as well as passing?
items.a: Funded account management is a different service with a different risk profile, because it puts someone else's hands on an account that pays you, and the funded document is separate from the evaluation one. We do not sell it as a standard option, and the same first step applies: the funded terms are read and the handling is agreed before anything is traded. What a pass leaves you with is your own account and your own decisions about it.

items.q: Can I pay to pass a prop firm challenge, or is that a scam?
items.a: Both exist, which is why the phrase needs splitting. Paying a provider to trade your evaluation is a real service with a real deliverable. Paying a firm to defer its own fee is a payment plan, and paying anyone for a guaranteed pass is a contradiction, because the outcome depends on a rulebook the provider does not control and can change mid-evaluation. The test in every case is the same two questions: what do you receive, and what does it cost if it fails?
